title: Take away the opinion
hook: take away "I've been harmed," and the harm is gone (Meditations 4.7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: one city. Your line was one city. Which stranger did you treat as a neighbor? Day five hundred fifty-three, the end of a week.

A friend forgets your birthday. That's the event. Within an hour it has a title: they don't care about me. By evening it has a sequel: nobody really does. The event took one second. The title has been running for days. A grievance can work like this: a small fact, and a big label stuck on top of it. Marcus Aurelius wrote two short sentences about peeling the label off. Today: take away the opinion.
screen: `A FORGOTTEN BIRTHDAY.` → `THE TITLE: THEY DON'T CARE.` → `TAKE AWAY THE OPINION.`

segments.voice: First, the chain. In the seventh entry of book four, Marcus writes, in effect: take away your opinion, and the complaint I have been harmed is taken away. Take away the complaint, I have been harmed, and the harm is taken away. Three links: the opinion makes the complaint, and the complaint makes the harm. Second, what he means by harm. This is not a claim that broken bones don't hurt or that injustice isn't real. The very next entry explains. What doesn't make a person worse, he says, doesn't make their life worse, and doesn't harm them, outside or in. For a Stoic, the only real harm is to your character. In those terms, a forgotten birthday can't make anyone less honest or less kind. Only the response can. Third, the label. So the work is to notice where the event ends and the label begins. They forgot: event. They don't care about me: label. Take the label off and you're left with a smaller, truer thing, one you can actually deal with. Maybe with a phone call. Fourth, the week behind us. Tools ready: principles at hand. Help yourself now: act on your notes. Three parts: let the mind steer. Fuel: obstacles become material. On purpose: nothing at random. One city: strangers are neighbors. And now, take away the label. It sits underneath several of the others, since obstacles, strangers and cravings can all arrive with a label already attached.
screen: `OPINION, COMPLAINT, HARM.` · `WHAT DOESN'T MAKE YOU WORSE, ISN'T HARM.` · `EVENT, THEN LABEL.` · `THE WEEK BEHIND US.` · then, large: `TAKE AWAY THE LABEL.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one grievance you've been carrying, small or medium. Say the event in plain words: what actually happened. Then notice the label you added: disrespect, betrayal, typical. Now, just for this breath, set the label down beside you. Look at the event without it. What's left? Is there anything in it that makes you worse, unless you let it? The bell holds the time.
Take away the opinion. Marcus says remove the opinion and the complaint goes; remove the complaint, I have been harmed, and the harm goes. Today's word.
Your line: take away the label. When something stings today, split it in two: what happened, and what I'm calling it. Drop the second. Day five hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 4.7 by separating what happened from the label they've put on it, then setting the label down.

options: file it under betrayal and stay cold.
split the event from the label, then decide what to do.
fork.reveal: Marcus removes the opinion first. without the label, you can respond to the event, maybe by speaking up calmly.

original.note: Greek, 'I have been harmed': the complaint Marcus says to take away in 4.7.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't take things personally.
what it means: remove the opinion, and the complaint and the harm go with it.
what a scholar hears: Marcus's chain rests on the Stoic claim that only vice is truly bad, so only you can harm your own character.
